stories.title: 'Culture shift' needed in how UK does business, PM urges
stories.summary: Burnham says those who take risks should be backed by government, but his government has been criticised for increasing business costs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 13 September 2026

The UK needs a "culture shift" in how it does business, Andy Burnham has said ahead of a meeting between some of Britain's biggest bosses and the government.

The prime minister said those who take risks in business should be backed by government and local leaders should have the power to work with companies.

Burnham had been due to attend the meeting, but cancelled his engagements for Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father.

The Labour government has been criticised for increasing costs for firms, such as with the employer national insurance and minimum wage changes under Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The meeting comes as Chancellor John Healey prepares for his first Budget next month, with rising borrowing costs in recent weeks adding to the pressure on government finances.

Monday's gathering will include the heads of companies such as BP, Shell, HSBC, Morrisons, Sainsbury's, BT, Vodafone and Rolls-Royce.

Ahead of the meeting, Burnham said he would give people "the confidence that if they have a great idea, they'll get all the support they need to bring it to life".

"When local leaders have the tools to get things done and government works in partnership with business, you can pull in investment, create jobs and transform communities," he said.

He added the government would be "a partner for growth to make every part of Britain better off".

The meeting comes as higher borrowing costs in the UK and other countries present problems for governments looking to spend money on business support or investment.

Separately, hundreds of hospitality businesses have written to the prime minister , external , calling on him to cut VAT for the sector.

More than 800 pub, restaurant and hotel bosses - include celebrity chefs Heston Blumenthal and Tom Kerridge - signed the letter asking for the hospitality VAT rate to be reduced from 20% to 10%.

When he was still Mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham said he would argue for the tax to be in line with the lower rates seen in other European countries.

AI boom helps drive surprise UK growth in July Published 3 days ago

Why are petrol and diesel prices rising again? Published 3 hours ago

Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night Published 2 September

Official data revealed a surprise boost in the economy in July partly driven by artificial intelligence (AI) investment , though experts expect growth to slow in the months ahead due to high energy prices.

The US-Israel war with Iran has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices , affecting households and businesses.

The rise in energy costs has prompted fears that inflation will remain high and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep the pace of price rises under control.

The expectation of higher interest rates, as well as competition in the global debt market from AI firms looking to spend money on development, has driven up the cost of government borrowing in many countries.

However, many argue the UK has a particular problem. The UK yield for 10-year bonds, a key measure of government debt costs, is higher than countries such as the US, France, and Japan.

Experts say this is due to several factors affecting investor confidence in the UK, such as multiple prime ministers, chancellors and policy U-turns over a short period.

The boss of chip designer Fractile, Walter Goodwin, who will be attending the meeting on Monday, said the government's acknowledgement that high-growth businesses are crucial to job creation and the economy has been "a positive thing".

But speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said the UK could do better in attracting the best talent as the current system is "less dynamic" than other countries.

Goodwin said the UK should be attracting the best talent in the world, and mobility could be improved by reducing notice periods for when someone wants to change jobs from three months to a shorter timescale.

In an interview with the BBC last week, Healey called for a restoration of "confidence about Britain" despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs .

Others have argued that the Labour government has created its own problems by increasing costs for businesses.

Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "The way for the prime minister to get businesses thriving, delivering jobs and driving growth is to cut their taxes.

"Labour's jobs tax and employer red tape have been devastating for businesses. The consequence has been a drying-up of the jobs market, weaker investment and businesses facing ever greater costs."

stories.title: The real AI economy is being built by ordinary people
stories.summary: Far from Silicon Valley pitch decks, workers across Asia and Africa are bypassing tech industry hype to quietly rewire their daily jobs — one prompt, workflow, and local problem at a time.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Innovation

Far from Silicon Valley pitch decks, workers across Asia and Africa are bypassing tech industry hype to quietly rewire their daily jobs — one prompt, workflow, and local problem at a time.

Rest of World visited workers across Asia and Africa who are using AI to solve daily problems, make a living, and create new possibilities in their everyday lives.

These profiles reveal how people choose to leverage artificial intelligence — what they are willing to delegate, which tasks they insist on handling themselves — and how access to cheap, powerful AI can expand the limits of what one person can accomplish.

It’s proof the economic impact of AI is taking shape on a personal, local level as forces in Silicon Valley and China battle to command the global AI ecosystem.

🇳🇬 “I have invested my time but not my money”

When Nureeyah Ogunmuyiwa decided to hire her first employee earlier this year, she faced an unexpected problem.

The 24-year-old makeup artist, who caters to brides and bridal parties among others in Lagos, had never hired anyone before. With her business growing and Ogunmuyiwa stepping into content creation to promote her services, she knew she needed to hire help. But she didn’t know how to write a job description, what questions to ask in an interview, or what qualities to look for in candidates.

Ogunmuyiwa asked ChatGPT.

Within minutes, the chatbot produced a complete hiring plan, including interview questions and a checklist to evaluate candidates.

“ChatGPT was my hiring manager that made the process less of a hassle,” Ogunmuyiwa told Rest of World. “I told her that I needed someone reliable, and to let me know what to do and what to look out for. She gave me everything that helped me hire my amazing assistant.”

That assistant now works alongside the AI one.

Ogunmuyiwa first encountered ChatGPT a couple of years ago while working as a customer support officer at a Lagos logistics startup after graduating from university. She used it to rewrite emails so they sounded more empathetic to customers and professional to colleagues. When she left her job in 2024 to focus full time on the makeup business she had been building on the side since 2018, AI came with her.

As a bootstrapped entrepreneur with a small budget, she said ChatGPT has become her “most reliable business partner.” Today, it plays multiple roles.

It’s her social media manager, writing captions, suggesting suitable hashtags, and recommending content ideas that have helped attract new customers. It’s her sales coach, helping her refine client pitches so they sound “bold but not too salesy.”

It also handles the math. Whenever she restocks beauty products, ChatGPT helps her calculate prices based on costs and profit margins, saving hours of manual calculations.

“It saves me from punching each product in the calculator and then trying to do the mental work of arriving at a profitable price point,” Ogunmuyiwa said.

Nearly half of Nigeria’s population now has internet access, with the majority connecting through smartphones. Ogunmuyiwa finds the convenience of access to AI bots on her phone very useful.

ChatGPT has become one of her most visited apps, alongside WhatsApp Business and Instagram. She prompts it for the simplest tasks like setting reminders. She has organized her conversations with different labels: “Glam by Ree,” named after her business; “return to corporate” for her professional plans; and “my studio project” for creative planning.

When Ogunmuyiwa recently moved her business from her dining room to a rented studio, she used AI to generate mood boards, which she shared with carpenters and electricians as they worked on the new space.

As new AI tools appeared, she began experimenting beyond ChatGPT. After a friend recommended Anthropic’s Claude earlier this year, she reluctantly gave it a try, worried she’d have to teach another chatbot everything about her business from scratch. Eventually, she settled into using both but highly favors ChatGPT.

Ogunmuyiwa recently moved her business into a rented studio and used AI to generate mood boards.

Ogunmuyiwa shared AI-generated reference images with carpenters and electricians to design her new studio. Damilare Dosunmu

Despite relying on AI throughout her business, Ogunmuyiwa hasn’t paid for either service because she feels the free version serves her purpose.

“I have invested my time but not my money,” she said. “And I’m getting a great return.”

She is open to a paid version in the future if needed, especially to generate images and mood boards.

AI contributes roughly 5% to her business growth. “I can’t give all the credit to AI for giving my business structure because I made a personal decision,” Ogunmuyiwa said. “AI has really helped me to implement that structure in the best way possible. I spent less time on things I trust ChatGPT to handle.”

That growing dependence sometimes worries her.

At one point, she deliberately stopped using AI because she felt she was consulting it before making every decision. She tried using Google search instead.

“But Google, too, now has AI it’s promoting you to use,” she said. “It’s quite difficult to look anywhere these days without seeing AI.”

🇮🇳 “Let humans do that”

When Chinmayee Mishra opened Patta Chai, a neighborhood tea cafe on the outskirts of Bengaluru, she wasn’t trying to build a technology business.

Her husband, Ajay Anbalagan, had left his corporate career, and the couple wanted to create something deliberately slower: a cafe where people linger over chai, conversations, and freshly baked cookies. Their four-person staff knows regular customers by name. Every dish is plated by hand.

“If AI ever completely replaces the people cooking,” Mishra told Rest of World , “that’s the day I’ll shut down my cafe.”

Yet behind the handmade food and warm hospitality, Patta Chai has quietly become an unexpected experiment in grassroots AI adoption.

It began earlier this year with ChatGPT.

Like many small businesses, Mishra initially used it for marketing. Social media captions, which once required endless back-and-forth with an intern, now take minutes. She trained ChatGPT on her previous writing, asking it to mimic the reflective, long-form tone that has become part of the cafe’s identity.

Canva and Adobe Express, both equipped with AI features, helped her design labels, posters, and promotional material without hiring a designer.

The real transformation happened when she realized AI could do far more.

Although Mishra has spent years working in marketing at enterprise software company Zoho , she has no engineering background. Curious rather than technical, she began experimenting with AI tools by asking them questions, watching tutorials, and building one workflow at a time.

Soon, Mishra was building AI agents using Zoho’s Zia Agents platform — tools to automate tasks she currently handles through spreadsheets.

For instance, one of the agents she is testing analyzes daily sales and customer feedback. Another calculates recipe costs by combining ingredient prices, labor, electricity, and overheads before recommending a selling price. It even compares her prices with those of cafes within a 10-kilometre (6-mile) radius and makes suggestions based on similar menu items.

“The calculations were always possible,” Mishra said. “What AI adds is memory.”

Mishra, along with her husband Anbalagan, has created a deliberately slower business focused on handmade food and warm hospitality. Itika Sharma Punit

A live sales dashboard, built with Claude and hosted on Zoho Catalyst, pulls data directly from Patta Chai’s restaurant management software to show what’s selling and what’s not.

Instead of Mishra having to remember how she priced dozens of cakes or whether a new cookie resembles an older product, the AI assistant recalls previous decisions, compares ingredients, and offers pricing and menu recommendations in seconds.

It has also changed how the cafe communicates internally.

Mishra writes instructions for her staff in English and asks AI to translate them into Hindi or Bengali, allowing recipes and kitchen notes to move more easily across a multilingual team.

Every month, she pays around 2,000 rupees ($26) for ChatGPT Plus and 500 rupees for Canva Pro. Adobe Express costs her 2,500 rupees a year. The expenditure initially felt extravagant. Today, Mishra considers it one of her best business investments.

“It seems a little pricey if you are not doing anything with it,” Mishra said. “But I feel it is just brilliant because we get so much work done. You get a lot of value for that money.”

Not every AI suggestion makes it into the business. She trusts it with mathematics far more than judgment.

“If it’s a calculation based on my data, I trust it,” she said. “If it’s subjective — market positioning or emotions — that still has to be my intelligence.”

The cafe’s launch of samosas illustrates that balance. AI helped validate pricing and gave Mishra confidence that the margins worked. But the decision to introduce the dish — and the recipe itself — came entirely from the team.

Technology has also changed how she spends her workday. Hours once spent writing captions, updating spreadsheets, and calculating margins are now devoted to developing new menu items, organizing community events, and improving the customer experience.

Mishra remains cautious about letting AI reshape the cafe’s character. She rejected proposals for QR code menus, automated ordering screens, and AI-driven customer profiling. Her manager already remembers which regular likes less sugar in their coffee, she said.

“Let humans do that.”

Privacy and the environmental costs of AI rarely influence her day-to-day decisions, largely because she doesn’t believe her small business holds particularly sensitive information. Her concern lies elsewhere: ensuring technology stays behind the scenes.

For Patta Chai, AI isn’t replacing hospitality. It’s quietly taking over the paperwork so the team can focus on making tea.

🇨🇳 “Changed everyone at the bottom of the industry”

When Wendi Ma graduated from film school in New York in 2018, he imagined a career spent on bustling film sets, directing actors and working alongside cinematographers and lighting crews.

A decade later, the Chinese director spends much of his day writing AI prompts.

His production studio in Zhengzhou, central China, has no actors or camera operators. Instead, it employs people whose job is to generate thousands of AI video clips until one precisely fits the requirements of the scene.

Ma began directing minidramas just as the vertical, mobile-first format started taking off in China. His early titles, No Escape from My Ruthless Alpha and Twin’s Love Trap for Billionaire Dad , attracted tens of millions of views. By late 2023, Chinese-funded streaming apps such as ReelShort and DramaBox had brought the format to the U.S. , creating a global audience for the bite-sized soap operas.

Minidramas were considered low-budget, but it still took about $200,000, a crew of 50 people, and two months to make an entire series. Ma frequently traveled between New York and Los Angeles, directing live-action shoots with actors and full production crews.

Then AI video generation arrived.

By 2026, models such as ByteDance i ByteDance ByteDance is a Chinese internet technology company that owns TikTok and Douyin, a Chinese version of TikTok with a successful e-commerce arm. READ MORE ’s Seedance had become good enough for studios to produce entire dramas without hiring actors. Production companies rapidly shifted their investments toward AI-generated series, forcing directors like Ma to reinvent how they worked. Prompt writers, video generators, and editors have largely replaced traditional camera crews and lighting teams.

Today, Ma’s studio creates minidramas entirely with AI. He has rented an office space and bought laptops. To generate each second of video, Seedance charges about 0.8 to 1 yuan (12 to 15 cents). For the minidrama industry, the economics are impossible to ignore. It takes just 10 people, around $20,000, and less than a month to make a series.

“The transformation may not have reached the biggest productions yet,” Ma told Rest of World . “But it has already changed everyone at the bottom of the industry.”

A typical prompt might specify everything from the setting and camera angle to the emotions on each character’s face:

Medium close-up inside a hospital room. The baby starts crying. Asher picks her up and gently comforts her. Victoria watches him with a soft smile.

Prompt writers, video generators, and editors have largely replaced traditional camera crews and lighting teams in minidrama production. Courtesy of Wendi Ma

On each attempt, AI generates a different version of a scene, even with the same prompt. Finding the right shot often comes down to luck.

Prompts often include instructions like “realistic cinematic texture” or “handheld camera with a slight shake” to mimic live-action filmmaking. “Mostly it comes from imagination and experience,” Ma said of the art of writing prompts. “Or, the easiest way, you generate a clip and see if it works.”

Even then, there are no guarantees.

Every time the same prompt is submitted, the AI produces a different version of the scene. Finding the right shot often comes down to luck. That’s why the people generating videos have earned an unusual nickname: lottery masters.

To produce a 90-minute series, they may generate between four-and-a-half and six hours of footage before finding enough usable clips. Ma misses filmmaking the way he first learned it.

At a human shoot, the actors, cinematographers, and lighting crews brought their own artistic contributions, he said. “It felt like a chemical reaction was happening. It sparked subtle, accidental creativity.” Most of his old crew members have left the industry as jobs vanished.

🇮🇳 “It all depends on the content”

For years, Trishika Udyawar taught young children to dance using a library of existing songs. There was no shortage of music, but much of it felt outdated and generic.

Children’s dance songs often told students exactly what to do: Clap your hands, jump up, turn around. Udyawar’s employer, Rhythmus Happy Feet, wanted music that encouraged children to imagine rather than simply imitate.

The Mumbai-based dance education company develops curricula and trains teachers to conduct dance classes in more than 65 schools across India, and runs after-school dance programs.

Since January, Udyawar, 27, has been creating songs herself with help from AI.

She asks ChatGPT to draft lyrics that are aligned with classroom lessons. She then feeds the lyrics into AI music-creation app Suno, tweaking prompts repeatedly until the rhythm, language, and melody work for preschoolers.

In one of her AI-generated songs about the life cycle of a tree, children become seeds, then grow into big, sturdy trees. In another, they mimic insects moving through the monsoon.

“If I try to generate lyrics of one song, I probably have to do it 10 times before I get the exact output I need, and even then, I might have to make a few changes,” Udwayar, who works as a teacher and curriculum planner at Rhythmus Happy Feet, told Rest of World .

Before AI, Rhythmus relied on YouTube videos and licensed educational music. But licensing became expensive as the company’s curriculum expanded. “You have to buy rights for one class application, and to multiply by each class, the cost increases a lot,” Swara Patel, founder of Rhythmus Happy Feet, told Rest of World .

A music production company had quoted 60,000 rupees ($629) per song, and three months to create 10 original songs for Rhythmus.

With Suno, the dance company has made 60 songs in the same amount of time. Their annual subscription for the app costs around $90.

But Suno has recently come under fire for allegedly scraping millions of songs, including potentially copyrighted music, to train its AI model. It faces several lawsuits, including from Sony Music and Universal Music Group, because some of the AI-generated tracks bear a strong resemblance to existing hits. The company has admitted to using “essentially all music files of reasonable quality that are accessible on the open internet,” but claims it is fair use.

That hasn’t affected Rhythmus. Parents rarely ask where the songs come from, Udyawar said. “It all depends on the content of the song. If it’s nice, the lyrics are clean, the concept is great, the music is amazing, and it is appropriate, that’s all that matters.”

Before AI, Rhythmus relied on YouTube videos and licensed educational music. A music production company had quoted $629 per song to create 10 original songs. Ananya Bhattacharya

AI music-creation app Suno creates songs using lyrics provided to it. Making a rhythm and melody that would work for preschoolers requires several prompts.

Eventually, Rhythmus Happy Feet hopes to publish its growing catalogue of AI-generated music on streaming platforms like Spotify and Apple Music, and monetize it.

The company is also using AI to build a social media footprint.

In May, it started making AI-generated cartoon videos for Instagram to reach its intended audience — parents of young children. Some of these videos feature original songs created by Rhythmus. The videos are made using video-generation app Kling, for which the company spends around $130 per year. The Instagram page , called Easy Kids’ Dance, has amassed more than 33,000 followers.

Udyawar believes AI songs still require plenty of human work for now. She spends a lot of time refining prompts and rewriting lyrics.

The hard work is paying off, with schools appreciating the original songs and even making special requests. The principal of one school, impressed by a song for kids aged 3–6 years called “No More Screen,” asked for a tweaked version for older kids.

🇹🇼 “Enabled me to build things of my own”

On his way to meet a client, personal trainer Philip Yeh usually glances at his phone. Within minutes, he can see their workout history, where they struggled, and what to focus on that day.

A few months ago, those notes were scattered across different apps on his phone. It would take him at least 30 minutes to organize them each time. So Yeh, a 27-year-old from northern Taiwan with no coding experience, asked Anthropic’s Claude to help him build a better system.

The result is an AI-powered app called LinkOS that tracks clients’ workouts, summarizes their progress, and suggests what Yeh should focus on before every session. For him, the app is about much more than becoming a better trainer.

“AI has enabled me to build a life where I’m not just selling my labor hours, but to take back some control, and let me be a creator and build things of my own,” Yeh told Rest of World . “For a personal trainer, it is really important to have a clear record of the student’s progress to be able to make targeted judgments on how we assist them to achieve their goals. But sometimes, when there are more students, it is easy to lose track.”

Yeh began gravitating toward personal training while studying for a master’s degree in marketing management. He found teaching rewarding as he could help people attain their ideal physique and see them accomplish something their body could not previously do.

His goal is to build a career that gives him more control over his time and choices. For now, he describes himself as a “slasher” — someone who builds multiple careers instead of relying on a single full-time job.

By day, Yeh works in university administration. After work and on weekends, he trains six private clients across northern Taiwan, sometimes traveling an hour by train between sessions.

LinkOS, which he began building with Claude in June, stores each client’s workout history, goals, physical condition, and coaching notes. Claude is the only AI Yeh pays for — 600 New Taiwan dollars ($20) a month. He upgraded to the paid version because the free one repeatedly ran into token usage limits.

He eventually hopes to make LinkOS available to other trainers. After about a month of building its trial version, Yeh tested it with around 15 other personal trainers he met through social media. He is now incorporating their feedback before a second round of testing.

The app has improved Yeh’s efficiency. He estimates he can now accommodate three more clients. He emphasized that AI is not the only factor that has created this capacity.

Yeh, who had no prior coding experience, now hopes to make the app he built with Claude available to other trainers. Kinling Lo

LinkOS, built using Claude, stores the workout history, goals, physical conditions, and coaching notes of Yeh’s clients.

“My main consideration of whether or not I can take on more students is about whether or not I can afford the time,” Yeh said. “What AI helps me do is make sure that, within that time, I can still provide each student with quality training.”

Yeh uses AI to keep up with the science behind his training. He asks Claude to summarize the research he regularly receives from the U.S.-based National Strength and Conditioning Association, where he earned his trainer certification. AI also helps him consider how the research could apply to his training.

Still, there are parts of his job he would never hand over to AI.

“If a student tells me, ‘Coach, I can’t really feel the muscle strength used on this move on my left side,’ am I going to immediately open AI and ask it? Of course not,” Yeh said.

AI cannot tell whether someone has arrived exhausted after a stressful day at work, if the correct muscles are activating during an exercise, or if an injury requires changing a workout in real time. Those judgments, he said, still come from experience.

“I would still need to be doing my job.”

🇸🇬 “Helping compress the timeline by several years”

Every day, Shoumo Mitra helps decide what ends up on dinner plates around the world.

As a scientist at Corteva, a U.S. agricultural science company that develops seeds and crop protection products, Mitra studies whether new pesticides and treatments actually work on crops grown across Asia, Europe, and Africa. Farmers rely on those products to protect harvests from pests and disease, and his job is to make sure they deliver.

In recent years, artificial intelligence has become one of his most important research assistants.

Developing a new crop protection product can take seven to 10 years, generating thousands of pages of scientific reports, field trial results, and regulatory documents along the way. Rather than reading every document, Mitra now uses Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude to help him navigate years of accumulated work.

“AI is helping compress that timeline by several years,” 56-year-old Mitra, who is based in Singapore, told Rest of World . “It allows chemists to visualize and design candidate molecules more quickly, enables biologists to begin testing new compounds much earlier in the pipeline, and reduces the number of field trials needed.”

The technology has also changed where those trials happen.

To test a pest-fighting product, scientists need fields where the pest actually shows up, and pests rarely announce where they will strike. A trial planted in the wrong place can sit through a whole season without enough infestation to prove anything, forcing a second year of testing.

Mitra’s team now runs years of weather, soil, and harvest records through AI models that predict where a pest is most likely to hit, so trials land in the right fields the first time.

“By applying AI-based weather analysis and predictive modeling, we were able to pinpoint sites with a high likelihood of significant pest incidence,” said Mitra, Corteva’s Asia-Pacific head of strategic projects. “This not only improved trial site selection but also eliminated the need for a second year of trials.”

Developing a new crop protection product can take up to 10 years, but AI is helping shorten that timeline. Courtesy of Shoumo Mitra

Mitra often uses AI to compress thousands of pages of scientific reports, field trial results, and regulatory documents.

His trust in AI grew after Corteva signed a companywide agreement with Microsoft and rolled out its Copilot to 8,000 employees.

Its biggest impact, however, has been on the less glamorous parts of his job.

As a manager overseeing 16 people, Mitra used to spend nearly three weeks every year writing detailed performance reviews. Now he feeds Copilot notes about each employee, edits the draft it produces, and finishes the process in about a week.

“That’s a time savings of roughly 66%,” he said.

He uses AI throughout the workday. Copilot summarizes long email threads, drafts routine responses, and organizes reports. Even small courtesies run through the machine. When a team member recently completed five years with the company, Mitra fed ChatGPT a rough congratulatory line, asking it to make the draft warmer, then longer, until it sounded like him.

The trick, he said, lies in the asking.

“I spend more time crafting a detailed, well-thought-out prompt upfront than I do fine-tuning the response afterward,” he said.

Still, Copilot has its off days. Often, when its presentation slides leave him underwhelmed, Mitra hands the job to Claude, which has proved useful enough for him to personally pay for a subscription costing $200 a month.

His enthusiasm stops where company secrets begin.

Mitra keeps confidential material away from public tools, sticking to his company’s firewalled system for anything sensitive.

A recent consultation on corporate reporting prizes the interests of shareholders over society. It’s a step in the wrong direction

T he question of what corporations are for is deeply political. In a 1970 article for the New York Times, Milton Friedman argued that the “social responsibility of business is to increase its profits”. The idea that CEOs should worry about providing good jobs was “pure and unadulterated socialism”, he wrote. Friedman and his fellow neoliberals saw companies as vehicles for enforcing their politics. Their ideas endured: UK bosses are now paid 130 times more than average workers.

Despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism, a 12-week consultation recently launched by his government risks entrenching it. The consultation was first announced as part of the Starmer government’s crusade against “red tape”. The average annual report for some businesses now runs to 98,000 words, and no doubt there are areas that could be simplified. But the consultation proposes removing vital information and presumes that company reports primarily serve shareholders, rather than other stakeholders. Both are steps in the wrong direction.

The consultation proposes scrapping information about the ratio between CEO and worker pay, removing a vital benchmark for inequality. British CEOs already earn 95% more on average than their European equivalents, and opaque pay ratios only serve their interests. There is scant evidence that higher-paid CEOs create more productive firms. As one Harvard Law School paper observed, pay ratios show how much a company invests in its “human capital”, and matter to workers and investors alike. Consumers who are made aware of this information are more likely to choose products from firms where the ratio is lower, encouraging those firms to address glaring pay disparities.

The consultation reflects the idea that inequality within a company is immaterial, a perplexing stance for a government concerned with fairness. It suggests removing annual shareholder votes on director pay, on the basis that votes are still required every three years. Annual votes were a modest attempt from Theresa May’s Tory government to tame the “unacceptable face of capitalism”, and the GC100 lobby group of corporate leaders has called to scrap them. By giving way, Labour would be removing a Tory policy designed to rein in boardroom greed.

It also proposes allowing companies to shift towards fully virtual annual general meetings. Companies have been holding online AGMs since Covid, and the government suggests these can improve “accessibility”. This is misguided: such meetings tend to be shorter, and prevent shareholders from asking as many questions. In-person AGMs are an imperfect form of accountability, but confrontation is easier to avoid when people aren’t in the room. Earlier this year, more than 50% of BP shareholders voted against a resolution to replace in-person AGMs with online meetings. Shareholders and climate groups argued these were a threat to accountability .

If reporting is too onerous, it would be better to start afresh with a new regime that recognised the interests of workers and society at large. Some voluntary initiatives, such as B Corporations , already take a more holistic approach to the information they disclose. Even better would be a requirement to include workers on company boards and provide greater transparency on pay levels, including that of all executives and workers paid less than the living wage. As the legal professor Katharina Pistor observes, corporate law is a tool that creates inequality. If the government wants to end neoliberalism, it should scrap this consultation and start again.

Prime minister vows to ‘reindustrialise Britain’ through new partnership with business

The prime minister is to host business leaders, entrepreneurs and local mayors at Downing Street on Monday to pitch his government as a “partner for growth” that can offer a stable platform for investment and jobs in the UK.

Ahead of the event, Andy Burnham said the country had “everything it needs to succeed”, including talented people and world-class universities, but requires “a culture shift in how Britain does business” if it is to unlock its full potential.

The new prime minister vowed to “reindustrialise Britain” through a new partnership with business. “That means putting government firmly on the side of the people who take risks, start companies, create jobs and bring new ideas to life,” he said.

“It means ensuring ambition is rewarded, making it easier to start and grow a business and giving people the confidence that if they have a great idea, they’ll get all the support they need to bring it to life.”

Burnham will host a roundtable with entrepreneurs – including the founders of Octopus Energy, Revolut and Starling Bank and quantum computing companies including Oxford Quantum Circuits – before welcoming chief executives from some of Britain’s largest businesses for a reception in No 10 along with regional mayors.

They include the bosses of financial companies HSBC, Aviva and Standard Chartered, supermarkets Morrisons and Sainsbury’s, telecoms groups BT and Vodafone, oil companies BP and Shell and manufacturers Rolls-Royce and BAE Systems.

Monday’s round of meetings come as Burnham and John Healey , the chancellor, prepare for their first budget on 28 October.

Burnham has vowed to deliver growth across the country and to devolve power and resources away from Westminster to do so. But Healey faces a tough task, presenting his budget amid rising borrowing costs and the impact of the Iran war on the global economy.

Although the economy unexpectedly grew by 0.4% in July , boosted by AI and cloud computing, economists have warned rising energy costs may have held back growth in August and September.

Suren Thiru, chief economist for the Institute of Chartered Accountants England and Wales, said the chancellor could be left with a “budget headache” if economic growth starts to dwindle, as more muted growth and surging borrowing costs erode his fiscal headroom, raising the prospect of further tax rises.

Both Burnham and Healey have stressed their commitment to the fiscal rules laid down by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, which require day-to-day spending to be covered by taxes and government debt to fall as a share of the economy by 2029/30. They are also bound by Labour’s manifesto commitment not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT.

In his first major speech as chancellor last week, Healey said boosting economic growth would be his defining mission as chancellor but also warned Labour had to “be honest” about the need to control public spending at next month’s budget.

He talked of putting more power and resources into the hands of local leaders, reducing the cost of doing business and using public investment to attract private capital.

stories.title: Burnham cancels engagements after death of father
stories.summary: Burnham has previously said his father did not know he had become prime minister due to his Alzheimer's.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Burnham pictured with his parents, Eileen and Roy, after he was selected as Labour's candidate to become the mayor of Greater Manchester in 2016

Published 14 September 2026, 13:35 BST

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cancelled official engagements on Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's.

He had been due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street on Monday, and was expected to speak at the annual trade union TUC Congress in Brighton on Tuesday.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England .

He had also said his father's illness was so advanced that he did not know his son had become prime minister.

Speaking to the Times newspaper , external shortly before formally taking over as prime minister, Burnham said it was "a sadness, because he would be [proud]".

He continued: "The way I look at it, it's his achievement as well. A whole family achievement, although he doesn't know it."

The prime minister later said care home staff had shown his father footage of him entering Downing Street, calling it a "wonderful" thing.

Burnham said he wanted to help "my dad and the millions like him" when setting out plans to reform adult social care.

He said he had been "overwhelmed" by the skills and professionalism of care workers supporting his father.

Burnham has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In his 2024 book Look North, he wrote that neither of his parents had attended university, but could have done had they "grown up in a different time and different place".

"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go."

Opposition politicians have offered their condolences to Burnham and his family.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

"A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won't ever be the same again."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "My heart goes out to the prime minister on the loss of his dad.

"From our conversations he sounded like a wonderful man."

Green party leader Zack Polanski said: "There are moments in life such as this sad time that transcend politics and I join the whole country in sending condolences."

stories.title: I spent $4,000 on a robot dog from China
stories.summary: Unitree might be the world’s most important robotics company.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Unitree might be the world’s most important robotics company.

On a sunny morning in June, I walked to work with a quadruped robot beside me. I’ve never gotten more attention from strangers.

A bunch of people snapped pictures of my robot dog. Several people asked me questions. Was it mine? (Yes.) Did I build it? (No.) Was it being used for surveillance? (No.)

Biological dogs kept a safe distance from my mechanical companion. Some growled or barked at it.

Children were fascinated. I paused and had it do tricks for several of them: “shake hands,” do a handstand, or leap into the air.

I live in a leafy Washington, DC, neighborhood called Mount Pleasant. The neighborhood lives up to its name, so my morning commute is mostly downhill. My robot companion, manufactured by the Chinese company Unitree, walked the two miles to my office near the White House with battery capacity to spare.

I recharged the battery during the workday, but it still struggled on the afternoon walk home. We were now mostly walking uphill, and the temperature had risen to 87°F (30°C). The robot’s steps seemed increasingly labored as the path got steeper.

As I entered my own neighborhood, I glanced at two indicators in the corner of my phone screen. One showed that the robot’s battery was at 5 percent—dangerously close to empty. The other showed the internal temperature was 84°C (183°F).

We were within sight of my front door when the robot suddenly collapsed. I’m not sure if it ran out of power or overheated, but either way it didn’t shut down gracefully—it rolled onto its back with its legs in the air.

Several people have asked me what my robot is useful for, and the honest answer is not much.

Unitree quadrupeds are widely used for academic research, and they are sometimes used for entertainment . But there don’t seem to be a ton of practical applications.

Wheeled robots are faster and more energy-efficient, making them better for deliveries. Flying drones are a better choice for a lot of surveying and inspection work. My robot has no arms or hands, making it mostly useless around the house.

But my robot did have one big thing going for it: It was astonishingly cheap.

I paid $4,017. That’s more money than I’ve ever spent to review a product. But it’s also far less than I would have had to pay for this type of robot a few years ago. And it’s cheap enough that people may find uses for it that wouldn’t have made sense at higher prices.

Sometimes what changes the world isn’t the invention of a new technology; it’s figuring out how to make it affordable enough for a mass market. Xerox built the first personal computer with a graphical user interface, but companies like Apple, IBM, and Microsoft made the technology mainstream. Perhaps Unitree will play a similar role for quadruped robots—though, as I’ll discuss later, Unitree’s robots now face legal restrictions in the United States.

Unitree has also used quadruped robots as a stepping stone to another market that could be much more important—humanoids. Unitree launched its first humanoid robot in 2023. Leveraging its experience making cheap quadrupeds, Unitree is able to sell humanoid robots for as little as $13,500.

That’s still way out of my price range, which is why I bought a robot dog instead. But it’s dramatically cheaper than any humanoid you could buy a few years ago. And the low cost has made Unitree a global leader in humanoid robots.

Financial markets are bullish. Unitree debuted on the Shanghai stock market on August 19. On its first day of trading, shares shot up more than fivefold. It has lost some altitude since then, but at Monday’s closing price, the company was still valued at $34 billion—more than triple its valuation before the IPO.

How Unitree democratized legged robotics

Earlier in June, I visited Professor Xuesu Xiao, a roboticist at George Mason University.

“Ten years ago, only a very small set of research groups were working on quadruped locomotion because they were the only people on the planet who could build a quadruped,” Xiao told me. “Then Unitree came onto the market. And it basically democratized the entire world of quadruped locomotion research.”

Xiao gave me a tour of his lab, which had four Unitree quadrupeds. Each cost around $15,000. The lab also had a quadruped robot called Spot. It was made by Boston Dynamics—widely seen as the industry leader before Unitree came along. But Spot is expensive, starting around $75,000.

Unitree founder Wang Xingxing developed a crude quadruped robot called XDog for his master’s thesis at Shanghai University.

“ Marc Raibert from Boston Dynamics is my idol,” Wang told IEEE Spectrum in March 2016. “Their papers helped me to design XDog.”

Early Boston Dynamics prototypes—with names like BigDog and WildCat —had gasoline engines and hydraulic actuators. This made them too large, noisy, and polluting for practical use.

In that 2016 interview, Wang said that his goal was to “make quadruped robots simpler and smaller, so that they can help ordinary people with things like carrying objects or as companions.”

Boston Dynamics officially unveiled an electric quadruped called Spot in June 2016. But Spot didn’t become commercially available until 2020.

That created an opening for Unitree, which Wang founded in May 2016. The company’s first quadruped products— Laikago in 2017 and AlienGo in 2019—were powered by electric motors. Designed for research labs, they cost tens of thousands of dollars.

In 2021, Unitree launched the Go1 line , which started at $2,700 for the “Air” model. In 2023, Unitree unveiled the Go2 , which was even cheaper—$1,600 for the Air and $2,800 for the more capable Pro.

Today, Unitree’s cheapest robot—the Go2 Air—is more than 97 percent cheaper than Spot. But this is not an apples-to-apples comparison; Spot is larger than Unitree’s Go2 line and can carry heavier payloads.

Still, the fact remains that Unitree made quadruped robots affordable to many people who could never afford Spot—including me! My wife never would have let me spend $75,000 or even $15,000 on a robot dog. But I convinced her to let me spend $4,017 (after tariffs and shipping costs) on a Go2 Pro.

Why are Unitree robots so cheap?

Last year, the firm Simplexity tore a Go2 robot dog apart and made a video showing what they found.

Each of the robot’s four legs is powered by three motors. There’s a motor in the shoulder that controls the angle of the legs and a motor driving each of the two leg segments. “With three motors, you get a really dynamic range of motion,” said Luis Elenes, a mechanical engineer at Simplexity.

“They use all the same motors throughout,” Elenes added. “All four shoulders are identical in arrangement. There’s tons of benefit to that. There’s reduced cost, there’s reduced part count. The more you can reuse motors and reuse parts, the simpler your design gets, and the more robust overall your design will be.”

Jakub Bartoszek , an expert on motors and legged robots at the startup MAB Robotics , argues that Unitree also saved money by using low-quality components. The motors in Unitree robots—many of which are made in-house—tend to wear out more quickly than those in some other robot brands, he told me. But the cost savings make the robots affordable to more people.

Unitree seems to have designed its robots for easy repairs when they wear out.

“They want these legs to be serviceable in the field,” Elenes said. Thanks to the simple way the robot’s legs are attached to its body, “you can swap out a leg pretty easily. I would guess it would take you less than a minute.”

Unitree also gets significant support from the Chinese government, including tax credits and large-scale purchases by public institutions. It’s hard to quantify the scale of this support because the Chinese system blurs the line between public and private, military and civilian. But a supportive policy environment clearly helped Unitree to scale up its manufacturing operations and thereby drive down the cost of each robot.

How powerful motors enable cheap actuators

Unitree has another counterintuitive cost-saving strategy: using large and powerful motors. More powerful motors aren’t inherently cheaper, of course. But they allow Unitree to save money on another component called the reducer that can be even more expensive

Suppose you have a lever where one side is five times longer than the other. If you push the long side down by five inches, the short side goes up by just one inch. But force is magnified: 10 pounds on the long side becomes 50 pounds on the short side.

Many robots use gear systems called reducers that serve the same function; they convert the fast, relatively weak movement of an electric motor into a slower but stronger movement of a robot’s body parts.

Traditional industrial robots require extreme precision, so they tend to have large reduction ratios.

A page on the Boston Dynamics website , for example, indicates that two of the motors in Spot’s legs are paired with reducers that have gear ratios of 51 to 1. In other words, the motor would need to do 51 full rotations in order to produce one full rotation of a leg joint.

This enables Spot’s movements to be very precise while magnifying the power of Spot’s motors. But it also has some disadvantages. One is cost. Reducers with 51:1 ratios are complex and—as a result—tend to be significantly more expensive than reducers with lower ratios.

Another is rigidity. When a robot’s arm encounters physical resistance, it should yield gracefully—a property called backdriveability. It’s also helpful if a robot can sense this kind of physical resistance electrically. Robots with higher gear ratios perform badly on both these fronts; their limbs feel stiffer and they are less sensitive to physical resistance.

In contrast, Unitree uses large motors combined with a simple 6.33-to-1 gearbox. This makes its robots more nimble and dynamic while reducing costs. The simpler design is also easier to simulate, making Unitree robots easier to train.

Unitree’s decision to use a lower gear ratio is part of an industry-wide trend. High gear ratios made sense for industrial robots that were programmed to perform simple, repetitive motions. In contrast, many modern robots perform complex actions in unpredictable environments. This requires sophisticated control software that can respond flexibly to changing conditions. The software is constantly making small corrections anyway, so it can compensate for less precise hardware.

The humanoid pivot

One of the most impressive and crowd-pleasing capabilities of my Go2 Pro robot dog is handstands. The robot can balance on either its front or hind legs indefinitely, and can even move forward, backward, or side to side while doing so.

So it was natural for Unitree to expand into humanoids. Unitree first debuted a humanoid called the H1 in 2023. The next year, Unitree unveiled a cheaper and more capable robot called the G1.

I got to see one when I visited Xiao’s lab in June. He paid around $50,000 for a research-grade EDU version . The consumer version starts at $13,500. This is shockingly cheap given the robot’s capabilities.

A humanoid robot is more than a quadruped standing on its hind legs. My Go2 quadruped robot has three motors per leg, for a total of 12. The cheapest G1 humanoid has five motors in each arm, six in each leg, and one in the torso, for a total of 23. The leg motors in a humanoid robot also need to be more powerful, since it’s more work to balance on two legs than to stand on four.

Still, I suspect that Unitree’s experience with quadrupeds gave it a leg up on humanoids. By the early 2020s, Unitree had been shipping quadruped robots for several years. The company had deep expertise in actuator design and an extensive network of suppliers.

According to filings connected to Unitree’s August stock offering, the company’s quadruped revenue tripled between 2024 and 2025—from RMB 230 million ($34 million) to RMB 697 million ($104 million). The comparable figures for Unitree’s humanoids were RMB 107 million ($16 million) and RMB 867 million ($129 million)—an eightfold increase.

Humanoids accounted for 51 percent of Unitree’s revenue in 2025. I expect this figure to be even higher for 2026.

Unitree could have a durable advantage

“We are witnessing the birth of another Chinese hardware giant,” wrote a team at SemiAnalysis in June. “Three years ago, Unitree was a quadruped company. By last year, they parlayed quadruped dominance into creating and leading the humanoid market.”

The SemiAnalysis authors draw a parallel to DJI, the Chinese company that dominates the global drone market.

“DJI’s Phantom 1 shipped January 2013 at $679, and was not a fully-fledged product at the time,” the SemiAnalysis team writes. “It had no built-in camera, no gimbal (stabilizer), ten minutes of flight, no live video feed, but it was roughly half the cost of the build-it-yourself drone.”

Like DJI in 2013, Unitree’s robots today have a lot of rough edges. Certainly mine does.

The app to control the robot is buggy. Features Unitree showcased in its launch video —like climbing stairs and following a human owner—don’t work well in real life. If I turn the robot on with its legs slightly out of place, they will often thrash around wildly and the robot will wind up on its back.

Then there was the time my robot collapsed just feet from my house. A more polished product might have detected the low battery (or high temperature) and shut itself down gracefully.

But for bleeding-edge technologies, this kind of polish may not be very important. Far more important is getting costs down.

“DJI chose to inhouse the most expensive and technically difficult component first: the flight controller,” SemiAnalysis writes. “Later on, DJI brought inhouse the gimbals, motors, and ESCs.”

DJI figured out how to make these components more cheaply than they could be purchased from external suppliers, which in turn allowed it to undercut other drone makers. And that expanded the market for DJI’s drones.

Before DJI came along, “professional aerial photography was the domain of helicopters and Hollywood second-unit teams, but now, small businesses could perform this on their own. As such, whole new markets were unlocked for DJI, like real estate listings, wedding videos, local news, agricultural surveying.”

There’s a flywheel here: The more units a company sells, the better deals it can negotiate with suppliers and the more money it can spend optimizing its manufacturing process. Larger sales volumes also allow a company to bring more components in-house. This allows the company to push costs even lower, which will mean more sales and even more money to invest in improving the production process.

Over a few years, this flywheel helped DJI to dominate the global drone market. SemiAnalysis argues that Unitree is on track to do the same thing for legged robots.

According to SemiAnalysis, Unitree has developed its own motors, gearboxes, lidar sensors, and cameras. “Unitree’s self-produced motors can run as low as 30-40% of equivalent Western motors,” SemiAnalysis reports. “They now make some of the cheapest humanoid gearboxes in the world.”

This could enable Unitree to take over the global market for quadruped and humanoid robots in much the same way that DJI took over the global drone market.

Of course that’s not guaranteed to happen. Unitree has a number of Chinese rivals. Unitree is the global leader in quadrupeds, but a Chinese rival, AgiBot, has sold more humanoid robots than Unitree in recent months. There are also many smaller robot companies in China that could challenge Unitree and AgiBot in the coming years.

But Unitree does not face much competition in the United States or the West more generally. Boston Dynamics sells excellent robots, but they tend to be significantly more expensive. There are a number of American startups aiming to build humanoid robots, including Tesla, Figure, and 1X, but consumers cannot buy a robot from any of these companies today.

That has alarmed some American policymakers. In June, a bipartisan group in the House introduced a bill to restrict importation of Chinese robots. The official press release for the legislation mentioned Unitree by name. Then in July, the FCC imposed broad new regulations on foreign-made robots that are likely to impact Unitree and other Chinese companies.

However, the robot market is global. Even if Chinese companies get locked out of the US market, Unitree or one of its Chinese rivals could still come to dominate the global market for humanoid robots.

There’s an obvious parallel here to electric vehicles, where Chinese companies like BYD are effectively banned from the US but are making rapid gains in the rest of the world. There’s a risk that a ban on Chinese robots could have a similar impact: rather than hampering the growth of companies like Unitree, it could make the US a robotics backwater.

Tim Lee was on staff at Ars from 2017 to 2021. He recently launched a new newsletter, Understanding AI . It explores how AI works and how it’s changing our world. You can subscribe to his newsletter here .

stories.title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania woman died of measles complications, coroner says
stories.summary: The 40-year-old unvaccinated woman reportedly had underlying health conditions.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The 40-year-old unvaccinated woman reportedly had underlying health conditions.

A 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania, has died of complications from measles, according to the county’s coroner.

It marks the third vaccine-preventable, measles-linked death in the US this year. All three have occurred in Pennsylvania, which is experiencing an explosive outbreak that has caused over 670 cases and 124 hospitalizations across 37 counties . Prior to these deaths, Pennsylvania had not reported a measles death in 35 years.

In a news release dated September 12, Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong said the death of the woman was “a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease.”

The county’s chief deputy coroner, Jason Stiver, added that “this tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly.”

“Many people associate measles with a childhood illness, but it can lead to severe complications in individuals of any age,” Stiver said. “Measles is highly contagious and can result in serious respiratory illness, hospitalization, and in rare cases like this, death.”

Preliminary death certificate

While the news release stated that no additional information about the case would be provided, The New York Times obtained a preliminary death certificate. It indicated the woman had several chronic medical conditions, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and she required supplemental oxygen at all times. Her health status made her vulnerable to complications from measles.

The death certificate listed the immediate cause of death as respiratory failure “due to suspected measles.” Furlong told the Times that the woman’s measles case had yet to be confirmed by testing, but that she was unvaccinated and known to have been exposed to someone with measles. At the time of her death, she had many symptoms of measles, including the tell-tale rash, which often begins as red spots on the head or face and spreads down the body.

The news release noted that the coroner’s office is working with the state health department, which has not yet added the death to the state’s official outbreak tally. The health department provided a statement to The Washington Post saying that it was aware of the case.

“We are in touch with the coroner and appreciate his commitment to keeping the public informed,” the statement read. “The Department of Health is conducting a thorough review of this case and will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available.”

Two previous deaths in babies

The woman’s measles-linked death follows reports from the state’s health department of two others. Both occurred in babies in Lancaster County. Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, confirmed one of the deaths was in a 6-week-old baby girl who had a severe genetic condition. In that case, Diamantoni, a Republican-elected coroner in 2007, attributed the death directly to measles.

The other death was in a newborn boy, which the state counts as a measles-associated death under pre-determined case reporting guidelines. Diamantoni has publicly disputed that the death was due to measles, saying the baby was infected with measles but died of a ruptured spleen—which is a potential complication of measles. Overall, spleen ruptures are extremely rare in newborns, and Diamantoni has provided no other explanation for the organ’s failure. At the time of birth, the baby’s unvaccinated mother was severely ill with measles. The mother, the father, and their midwife all believed measles was the cause of the baby’s death.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention—which is under the control of anti-vaccine activist Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the current US health secretary—is not counting either of the two infant deaths in their measles data reporting. The agency cites a new requirement for reporting measles death that did not exist prior to events in Pennsylvania. The US Department of Health and Human Services did not respond earlier this month when Ars Technica inquired about the new rule.

Kennedy has publicly disputed the babies’ measles-linked deaths and got into a heated online exchange about them with Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro. In that exchange, Kennedy spread misinformation about the measles vaccine and claimed Shapiro “fabricated” the deaths.

Chinese president’s arrival in Delhi seen as step towards reconciliation after deadly 2020 military clash

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping , has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.

As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses. Later on Saturday, he was due to attend a gala dinner for the two-day summit.

The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi , who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.

The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which ‌20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.

Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently , with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.

Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.

This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.

Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.

But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.

On Saturday, the bloc managed to unanimously agree on the wording of a joint declaration that reiterated a commitment to peaceful resolution of international disputes “through dialogue, consultation and diplomacy”.

The “New Delhi declaration” ​called for “maximum restraint” in the Middle East, although it was worded so as not to call out member countries actively involved in conflicts.

Jiang Shixue, the vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.

“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.

Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.

China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.

India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.

Saturday’s talks began with an address by Modi, who said Brics was “not against anyone”.

Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.

“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.

“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

stories.title: Yuja review – portrait of star pianist who is intellectually curious and deeply musically attuned
stories.summary: Musician is also rattled to find her appearance gets far more attention than her playing in this reflective documentary from Lorna Tucker As well as her film about her own difficult teenage years , British director Lorna Tucker is probably best known for her documentaries on famous women with big personalities: Vivienne Westwood ( Westwood: Punk, Icon, Activist ), Katharine Hepburn (Call Me Kate) and Greta Garbo ( Garbo: Where Did You Go? ). Her latest subject, pianist Yuja Wang, is another high-achiever – but not someone with quite the same name recognition unless you’re a devotee of classical music, a field in which she is ranked among the very best alive. Wang certainly has a flamboyant side, expressed in her highly expressive, virtuoso performances and her sartorial style on stage. In fact some shocking pull quotes illustrate how her dress sense has been bizarrely over-examined in the press; she has been likened to a stripper for her outfits, and the New Yorker, of all publications, once described her as “fat” , which hardly seems germane to any discussion of her ability to play Tchaikovsky or Ligeti. But Wang’s biography and the texture of her daily life are very different from that of Tucker’s previous subjects. She was a child prodigy from an artistic Beijing family who came of age just in time to break records for views on YouTube. Sure, her life here looks glamorous in one way, with a lush New York apartment she barely ever sees because she’s constantly on the road. But her life is also one of perpetual practice and striving for perfection, the loneliness of the long-distance soloist. stories.title: Governor Newsom Signs Student-Backed Digital Literacy Bills Alongside Misguided Bans
stories.summary: Governor Newsom signed a package of 12 bills yesterday aimed at “protecting children” online. One of them was AB 1709 , which EFF has opposed this legislative session and serves as a functional ban on young people under 16 using social media. However, EFF supported two of the bills signed into law, AB 2071 and AB 2298 , which require that children learn critical digital literacy and cybersecurity topics. The bills are an affirmative and constitutional way for the state to address valid concerns about young people’s internet use without violating their First Amendment rights . Unlike blanket bans , A.B. 2071 and A.B. 2298 address online safety through education rather than prohibition. Young people rely on the internet not just for entertainment, but for civic engagement , education , self-expression , and community —especially vulnerable youth who may lack support in their physical surroundings. This is why real digital safety comes from preparation, not isolation. Research consistently shows that open, honest conversations about digital literacy and privacy with trusted adults are far more effective at protecting youth than restrictive censorship laws. Young people themselves recognize this need; in fact, A.B. 2071 was co-authored by a group of students actively seeking better resources to navigate their digital lives safely. Education vs. Censorship A.B. 2071 and A.B. 2298 fill critical gaps in California’s school curricula by equipping students with actionable skills. A.B. 2071 integrates digital wellness into middle and high school health classes, teaching students how to identify unhealthy tech habits, protect their personal safety, and evaluate digital content—including AI-generated media—for credibility and bias. Meanwhile, A.B. 2298 adds cybersecurity concepts to recommended school curricula, teaching young people how to safeguard their personal data from online threats. While the state’s turn toward social media bans remains a harmful and misguided policy direction, the passage and signing of A.B. 2071 and A.B. 2298 show there is a better way. Lawmakers must stop treating censorship as a quick fix and instead focus on constitutional, empowering solutions that give youth the tools they need to thrive online.

stories.title: Cold TAKE: Amazon's New Encryption Method Still Doesn't Deliver Real Privacy
stories.summary: Amazon recently debuted a new feature for its Ring cameras that the company is calling Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The idea is to cut back on the amount of video content available to the company, and thus potentially available to law enforcement. But while it might technically add a speed bump to accessing full video content, it doesn’t deliver nearly the level of privacy we should be demanding from video doorbells and other security cameras. TAKE introduces a new way for Ring to manage encryption keys, where the user’s device has its key, then the company holds encryption keys temporarily within its own cloud infrastructure. Ring’s servers receive the keys temporarily so it can offer a variety of the features it says it can’t offer when a user chooses to use end-to-end encryption, like video descriptions, smart alerts, video search, and more , then deletes the key after 24 hours. This differs from how it works now, where footage is encrypted in transit and at rest, then decrypted by Ring, which always has access to the footage, to process those features. Comparatively, this is an improvement to the default settings Ring has now, because it at least puts some restrictions on historical footage, but it has some serious holes worth exploring. Ring Gets Access to Unencrypted Video for a Short Period Ring has designed its service so many of its camera features, including smart alerts and video search, need cloud processing to work. That means to provide those features, Ring needs to decrypt the footage while it’s stored in Ring’s cloud servers. With TAKE, in order to decrypt footage to offer these features, Ring gets access to footage stored in the cloud for 24 hours. TAKE adds some small measures using secure enclaves to make base key material harder to directly export, but keys are still released to services that can be modified. With access to the keys, the cloud processing does its thing and delivers the requested feature to the user. The key is then deleted 24 hours later—until the user wants to watch an old video or use other so-called “smart” features, at which point the keys are sent back to the server. In practice, that makes the system as a whole barely different from encryption at rest where the server holds the keys. The client device essentially takes the place of a hardware security module (HSM) , including making those keys available…
